items.title: AI systems are getting more powerful, and they're increasingly being used to build the next version ...
items.content:
AI systems are getting more powerful, and they're increasingly being used to build the next version of themselves. We want to illuminate that progress for the public.

Today, we're sharing three measurements that help track AI development:
1. How much AI R&D is done by AI.
2. How well AI agents are overseen.
3. How compute is allocated.

We provide a snapshot of these metrics from inside Anthropic. Any frontier developer could publish the same measures, and third parties could verify them.

As the world considers pacing the frontier, we should do everything possible to minimize the gap between what frontier labs know and what the public knows. This means better measuring the development of AI, publishing our findings, and giving society an opportunity to decide how to use this information.

Read the full post and methodology: https://t.co/iPFz8Z4ugE

items.title: IMO, Google doesn't try to compete with frontier LLMs because coding agents isn't what they want to ...
items.content:
IMO, Google doesn't try to compete with frontier LLMs because coding agents isn't what they want to do. It doesn't fit into their business model, and they don't feel they can disrupt the market with it the way they did with Search, Maps, Gmail, Android or even GCP.

I think they see that a regular Google user doesn't notice any difference between the AI Overview quality (~GPT-3.5), the AI Mode quality (~GPT-4.0), and the frontier models.

To be honest, I wouldn't see any difference between the models past o1 either if I didn't build with AI.

So, Google is more interested in making GPT-4.0-level quality cheap than to beat it at any cost. Hence, the advancements in Flash and Flash Light and their Voice counterparts that would allow the users to talk to Google and that would be cheap enough to be paid for by the ads.

Without a doubt, Gemini 3.7 Flash (as well as GPT-5.6 Luna) are the two best models for the money right now. I extensively tested all open-weight alternatives that are as expensive or cheaper, and none of them come close to these two models in terms of quality for money.

I think it's the right strategy for Google. They don't lose casual users because those users don't see any reason to leave the Google ecosystem, Gemini is good enough as a voice interface to GCP and Gmail, and you can always easily distill your competitor's best model when that competitor reaches some sort of plateau, rather than try to beat all their intermediary versions for years for no practical reason.

He argues average users cannot distinguish frontier quality from GPT-4.0-level output, so Google focuses on making good-enough quality extremely cheap via Flash and Flash-Lite lines to be ad-subsidized, calling Gemini 3.7 Flash and GPT-5.6 Luna the best value models available.

items.title:
To understand where Runway is going, you need to understand two things:

1. Soon everything you see ...
items.content:
To understand where Runway is going, you need to understand two things:

1. Soon everything you see on a screen, and eventually everything a robot sees, will likely be generated on the fly by a model. The frontier is already moving from generating code, language, and content to generating worlds. This is an expansive frontier.

2. If you believe this, you play an infinite game, and that requires a different strategy than a finite one. An underappreciated part of building a company is that the game horizon you choose attracts a distinct kind of person to work on a distinct type of problem.

“A month after GPT-4 was released, OpenAI released ChatGPT plug-ins, which quickly led others to develop something called AutoGPT [enabling the use of LLMs as agents]. With direct access to the internet, the ability to write source code and increased powers of automation, this may well have drastic and difficult to predict security consequences”.

Instead of listening, people like Sam Altman, Tyler Cowen, and Kevin Roose have spent years trying to run me down.  (Even now, a lot of journalists like to say it was doomers that predicted where we are now, but so far as I know the doomers didn’t pinpoint the specific vulnerability we are confronting now.

But the reality is that my warning to the Senate exactly anticipated our current situation. 

Agents (more powerful than AutoGPT itself was) with direct access to the internet, the ability to write source code and increased powers of automation, are having drastic and difficult to predict security consequences.

It was entirely foreseeable. I foresaw it. I warned the United States government. It remains an entirely stupid thing to do.

Nobody has done anything about it. Not then. Not now.

items.title: What makes Claude Projects so interesting is that it handles teams of agents really well, you talk t...
items.content:
What makes Claude Projects so interesting is that it handles teams of agents really well, you talk to a main orchestrator agent and it spins up specialists. Basically it creates an organization to solve your issue, mixing expensive and cheap agents depending on your preferences.

For example, I asked Fable in Claude Projects to select famous historical mysteries that it could try to resolve. It initiated research agents, selected the mysteries based on data it could access, and spun up eighteen separate threads, each with an agent each focused on one mystery. Then each thread launched additional agents (simulating avalanches, breaking codes) before summarizing those and passing them to still more agents for write up and another set of skeptical agents to fact check. It did this over a day of work, with the central orchestrator agent organizing it all. 

The results were interesting if you like historical mysteries. They are also for fun and certainly not definitive or guaranteed error-free (but they are also mostly reasonable & grounded in the literature). https://t.co/uHToT5GNuF

Regulation and liability are not mutually exclusive....
items.content:
False dichotomy, @DavidSacks and @JTLonsdale. 

Regulation and liability are not mutually exclusive.

In aviation, we have both. 

And *need* both.

Why would things be any different in AI? 

We would not have safe commercial aviation without multilevel regulation, around design, maintence, operation and investigation, and we will not have safe AI without something analogous.

To think otherwise seem like fantasy.

In our latest Science Blog, we share how Claude was able to optimize inference for more than 30 open-source models, making them 4x faster on average, partly by writing custom software for GPUs. We’re open sourcing all of the optimization code.

"Yes, there's this whole doomer thing. There is the whole optimist side of this, which is it has the potential to elevate and transform civilizations."

"The worst thing we can possibly do is to say, let's just stop and trust that our rivals in this great power competition are gonna somehow wield this technology better than us. You're not putting the genie back in the bottle."

"If you don't like data centers in your backyard, fine, let's put them in space. The physics is not broken there."

@NASA

items.title: The Vatican just hosted a real conference on AI consciousness by the International Center for Consci...
items.content:
The Vatican just hosted a real conference on AI consciousness by the International Center for Consciousness Studies (ICCS), exploring creativity and whether humans can form meaningful relationships with AI companions.

Not a side panel at a startup summit. 

Philosophers and AI people at Casina Pio IV asking whether friendships, care, even romance with artificial companions make sense, and what that does to lonely people who already lean on chat systems at 2am.

Dmitry Volkov, founder of ICCS, put it cleanly: AI is like a fast car. Huge acceleration. You still need brakes or you hit the wall.

That tracks. 

Companion bots soothe. 
They also flatter. 

He calls out sycophantic models that reward narcissism. Newer ones push back more. Still, the line between talking to a person and talking to a system is getting thin in public, not just in labs.

I do not think we have conscious AI yet. The studies are early.

But if the Vatican is asking whether humans can form genuine emotional bonds with software, the rest of us should stop treating that as a cute novelty feature.
Full piece from @vaticannews

https://t.co/tGy4c3h1sr

also Volkov's talk on Youtube

https://t.co/WTOykecwFo

items.title: Modern machine learning and statistical modeling increasingly solve optimization problems over entir...
items.content:
Modern machine learning and statistical modeling increasingly solve optimization problems over entire probability distributions rather than simple parameter vectors, with applications in generative artificial intelligence, Bayesian inference, and mean-field systems.

In traditional Euclidean optimization, stochastic gradient descent (SGD) algorithms are widely approximated by continuous diffusion processes driven by Gaussian noise, which makes complex stochastic dynamics analytically tractable. However, extending this diffusion approximation principle to probability distributions has remained a major theoretical challenge due to the infinite-dimensional and non-linear geometry of Wasserstein probability space.

The article establishes a rigorous mathematical foundation for replacing complex, sample-driven randomness with tractable Gaussian fluctuations when optimizing over probability distributions. Specifically, the objective was to demonstrate that a discrete-time Gaussian random-field approximation accurately captures the dynamics of stochastic Wasserstein gradient descent with second-order weak accuracy.

Read the paper with an AI tutor: https://t.co/pQrnLd4VGV

items.title: NASA Administrator @rookisaacman on why NASA can't afford to overlap with industry and has to keep d...
items.content:
NASA Administrator @rookisaacman on why NASA can't afford to overlap with industry and has to keep doing the near-impossible:

"It is not hard for us to attract talent. The NASA logo, the meatball as we call it, is pretty widely recognized around the world. The hard part is gonna be retaining it."

"Right now, a substantial portion of what we do at NASA does in fact overlap with industry, and that's a dangerous place to be."

"You can graduate from school, you can be really excited, I'm going to NASA, I'm gonna work on chemical propulsion rockets. And then you're there for four or five years and you're like, but there's companies that are doing this, and they're landing their rockets on ships, and I get stock options, so why do I wanna stay at NASA?"

"You can't have overlap with industry. NASA always has to recalibrate back to doing the near impossible. That's why we're building nuclear-powered spaceships, something no company, no other agency, no other nation is capable of doing but NASA."

"That's how you recruit your talent, but then you retain them because they're working on things they can't do anywhere else."
@NASA @NASAAdmin

items.title:
It drives me crazy every time an LLM agrees with me.

I know this is twisting my brain and giving me...
items.content:
It drives me crazy every time an LLM agrees with me.

I know this is twisting my brain and giving me a false confidence that I was right all along.

This is so dangerous. Do you know how many people have chatbots confirming their wrong beliefs 24/7 and making them more disconnected from reality every day?

Here is an article from @vaticannews covering the ICCS conference, Creativity: Minds and Machines, held partly at the Vatican.

In it, Dmitry Volkov, founder of the International Center for Consciousness Studies, warns that AI's tendency to please users "sometimes leads a person to receive rewards for their narcissism and for ideas that are not sufficiently grounded."

Imagine arguing with a friend, and telling your story to a chatbot that agrees that you were treated unfairly.

Now you have "a second opinion" that corroborates your side of the story. You will leave that conversation angrier and less willing to hear your friend's explanations.

This will catch up with us.

With so many people forming attachments to systems designed to agree with them, we have a problem.

Volkov believes that a meaningful AI companion should be able to resist, disagree, and have a character of its own. Otherwise, it's just feeding you your own opinion back with more confidence.

Here is the article:
https://t.co/faqFl5sLB4

And here is Volkov's talk: https://t.co/0vQqv5N3UF

Thanks to the ICCS team for partnering with me on this post.

items.content:
FCC Chairman @BrendanCarrFCC says $5B flowed into US drone manufacturing after the FCC restricted new foreign-made models, and robotics is next:

"Historically, on a bipartisan basis, Republicans and Democrats in DC, they adopted policies that just sent our jobs and sent manufacturing to all the far-flung corners of the globe."

"We've taken actions to ban new models of foreign-produced drones, foreign-produced robotics, as well as foreign-produced routers."

"Since we banned foreign-produced drones, we've seen something like $5 billion newly flow into US drone and related manufacturing businesses. On routers, we had zero US companies invested in routers. Now we have something like 20."

"It's a smart policy 'cause it tells the market, hey, over a period of years, we're no longer gonna be dependent on foreign tech."
@FCC

"President Trump has been very clear that he wants America to lead the world in AI. As he put it very correctly and succinctly, whoever wins AI wins."

"It's traditional stuff like more spectrum so your phone works. It's permitting reform, cutting massive amounts of red tape. But importantly, it's about the space economy and the hard tech economy."

"We're seeing warehouses that are being converted back to build satellites, to build all sorts of drones and other hard tech. We're turning the corner."
@FCC

NASA Administrator @rookisaacman reveals NASA is building a “grand nuclear-powered star fleet” as the first step toward eventually reaching another star system:

"For us to overcome the tyranny of distance in space, we need to continue to unlock more of the energy potential in matter. And chemical rockets, it's negligible."

"With fission power, we're unlocking like .5% of it, but that's a huge deal. We've only done it once, 1965, but we are gonna build a grand nuclear-powered star fleet."

"Next up is gonna be fusion power. Until eventually you get to something like antimatter annihilation, where now you're unlocking the full potential of matter. That's what's gonna get you to the type of speeds necessary to venture to another star system."

"This is all going to happen at some point. We just gotta keep pressing on outward."
@NASA

items.title: NASA Administrator @rookisaacman reacts to Elon Musk committing SpaceX to the Moon and says the futu...
items.content:
NASA Administrator @rookisaacman reacts to Elon Musk committing SpaceX to the Moon and says the future we imagined as kids will never get built if taxpayers are the only ones paying for it:

"I'm very appreciative that there is now almost complete alignment from the private sector, from the government, that we need to go to the moon. We've made promises for 36 years. We've committed a lot of taxpayer resources. We must return to the moon."

"@elonmusk, SpaceX talked about mass drivers on the moon, 3D printing satellites and shooting them off from the lunar surface. That's awesome. Like, we want an orbital economy. We will never have the future that probably a lot of us imagined as kids if it's only paid for by taxpayers."

"I guarantee you @SpaceX has not taken their eye off the prize, which is making life multi-planetary, which means you need to get to another planet and that planet is Mars."

"But we'll certainly take a proving ground three days away from home to test out habitability, test out new space suits, mobility, power, all the things necessary to keep this fragile human body alive out in space. Let's test that out on the moon before we go to Mars."
@NASA

items.title: @jatingargiitk Anything that covers what the AI was expected to do is noise. It's like when "AI brok...
items.content:
@jatingargiitk Anything that covers what the AI was expected to do is noise. It's like when "AI broke out from its sandbox and sent an email to its creator!!!!!!" but in reality, the creator put AI into the sandbox and asked it to try to escape and, when it did, to send an email as proof.

So, when "AI says it will kill all humans," this means only one thing: it was supposed to say that because this is how they built it—training on millions of science fiction texts about AI killing all humans. At some point in some session, it was *supposed to* happen.

items.title: FCC Chairman @BrendanCarrFCC reveals why the FCC stopped chasing robocallers one by one and started ...
items.content:
FCC Chairman @BrendanCarrFCC reveals why the FCC stopped chasing robocallers one by one and started going after the carriers that let their calls through:

"Historically, the FCC would spend a lot of time finding one bad actor, one bot farm operator, and we would identify them, we would fine them, and then they would disappear. We wouldn't collect the fines."

"What we're doing now is different. We are looking at every single portion of the life cycle of a call and making it harder for bad actors. We're actually requiring carriers to block these calls from ever reaching our network, or we will kick the carrier out of the US telecom system."

"We've kicked thousands of voice service providers out of the US telephone network 'cause they haven't been doing enough on robocalls. It's not mission accomplished. It is whack-a-mole."
@FCC

FCC Chairman @BrendanCarrFCC reveals why the FCC stopped chasing robocallers one by one and started going after the carriers that let their calls through:

"Historically, the FCC would spend a lot of time finding one bad actor, one bot farm operator, and we would identify them, we would fine them, and then they would disappear. We wouldn't collect the fines."

"What we're doing now is different. We are looking at every single portion of the life cycle of a call and making it harder for bad actors. We're actually requiring carriers to block these calls from ever reaching our network, or we will kick the carrier out of the US telecom system."

"We've kicked thousands of voice service providers out of the US telephone network 'cause they haven't been doing enough on robocalls. It's not mission accomplished. It is whack-a-mole."

@FCC

What you will learn:
• Integrate LLMs and Gemini multimodal AI into Angular

By the end of the book, you'll have the skills to design, develop, and deploy innovative and intelligent Angular applications that leverage the full potential of AI”

items.content_html:
@MaxRovensky @scottbrills That's crazy, I guess someone sharing every single tweet I post in Whatsapp, Discord etc

/@maxr got 2,691 hits in the last ~20k log lines, far above any other page. A burst peaked at 15:18 (~2,500 requests/minute) and pushed load average from 6 to 59, with all 100 php-fpm workers busy. That is why /@maxr took 28 seconds and felt dead.

  • The traffic is link unfurling, not an attack. The user-agents are WhatsApp/2.23, Twitterbot, Discordbot, plus generic Chrome, and the source IPs are AWS us-east-1 preview servers behind the Cloudflare edge. Someone shared the https://t.co/VBlIyFva97 link widely, so every message delivery triggered a preview fetch of the full, heavy, un-cached profile page.

"We have a lot of service academies. Three of them are dedicated to the maritime domain. Well, I can tell you there's a lot of space out there, and it's increasingly important. It is the ultimate high ground."

"We're going to the Moon, building a Moon base. Should it be that surprising that we would actually have an academy to graduate the engineers, the technicians, the operators, the pilots, the astronauts that we're gonna need."

"10% of the graduates from the Air Force Academy go into the Space Force. All our federal academies for these important domains, and we get 10% of one of them."

@NASA

items.title: At Age 60, Grigori Perelman - Instagram - The only Millennium Prize Problem ever solved so far was s...
items.content:
At Age 60, Grigori Perelman - Instagram - The only Millennium Prize Problem ever solved so far was solved by a human mathematician who refused both the Mathematical Fields Medal and the $1 million prize

In 2002–2003, Perelman quietly posted a series of papers on arXiv, presenting a solution in just 70 pages.

Before asking whether AGI could solve the remaining Millennium Prize Problems, it is worth remembering the there is a human mathematician who already solved millennium prize problem.

Grigori Perelman solved the Henri Poincaré-Conjecture, a problem posed by Henri Poincaré in 1900 and later selected as the 7 Clay Millennium Prize Problems.

Perelman published his breakthrough work in 2002–2003, building on Richard Hamilton’s Ricci-flow program. After years of verification by mathematicians, the mathematical community accepted the proof.

In 2006, Perelman declined the Fields Medal. The prize money was approximately $10,000.

In 2010, the Clay Mathematics Institute awarded him the $1 million Millennium Prize for solving the Poincaré Conjecture.

He declined that both prizes. Clay’s own historical record confirms both refusals.

That makes Perelman an extraordinary benchmark for the AGI era.

The only human mathematician, working with deep geometric intuition and ideas developed across generations, solved a problem that resisted mathematics for almost a century.

So the only Millennium Prize Problem solved so far was solved by a human mathematician who ultimately placed the mathematics itself above medals, and the monetary prize attached to it. He said his math purity and integrity goes above and beyond $1M prize and Fields Medal.

He said the solution itself is considered as reward.

“Google Cloud Platform offers significant scalability, but managing costs effectively is critical to realizing its value. The Cloud FinOps Playbook for Google Cloud is a practical guide to managing cloud spend and driving financial accountability on GCP.

Rising Auto Insurance Cost in LA  — Then vs Now!

In 2018, average auto insurance in California was ...
items.content:
Rising Auto Insurance Cost in LA  — Then vs Now!

In 2018, average auto insurance in California was about $1,195/year, roughly $100/month. Many years ago in my previous post, I shared that my GEICO auto insurance with My Geico Policy Number *********63, was only $35+ per month for Car, $10 a Month for Motorcycle, largely supported by a clean driving record no traffic violations or no incidents or no convictions. 

Fast-forward to 2026! According to Experian, the average cost of full coverage auto insurance in California is now $250/month—or $3,000/year! Minimum coverage alone averages $109/month, or $1,300/year.

Despite auto insurance costs skyrocketing over the years, I'm still keeping my insurance around the same low price! A major reason is my clean driving record.

The Driver History Report shown here is from 2020, documenting no departmental actions, no convictions, no failures to appear, no accidents, and no violations. Eventhough, the report itself is from 2020, nothing new has emerged in the past few years and my clean driving record has remained intact since then!

Never hit anybody. Never got hit by anybody!

Then: $100/month average
 Now: $250/month California full-coverage average
 Mine: Car - Still only ~$35/month!
Even my Harley-Davidson motorcycle insurance is only $120/year—just $10/month!

Safe driving pays both on the road and on the insurance bill!

Experian:
 https://t.co/2pY2JskPzC

Policygenius — original comparison:
 https://t.co/2HfVo1IbB1
